blocks.how_it_works: New Jersey's certification of trust is governed by N.J.S.A. 3B:31-81 under the New Jersey Uniform Trust Code (N.J.S.A. 3B:31-1 through 3B:31-84, enacted 2015, effective January 1, 2016). The statute provides that instead of furnishing the trust instrument to a non-beneficiary, the trustee may furnish a certification of trust containing: that the trust exists and the date the trust instrument was executed; the identity of the settlor; the identity and address of the currently acting trustee; the powers of the trustee; the revocability or irrevocability of the trust and the identity of any person holding a power to revoke; the authority of co-trustees to sign and whether all or less than all are required to exercise trustee powers; and the name in which title to trust property may be taken. The certification must be signed by all persons identified as currently acting as trustee. It must state that the trust has not been revoked, modified, or amended in any manner that would cause the representations to be incorrect.

faq.q: Does New Jersey require the trust's taxpayer identification number in the certification?
faq.a: No. Unlike the model Uniform Trust Code and some UTC states such as Missouri and Nebraska, New Jersey does not include the trust's taxpayer identification number in the required contents of the certification under N.J.S.A. 3B:31-81. The NJ UTC also does not require the manner of taking title to trust property, only the name in which title may be taken. These omissions distinguish the NJ certification from the standard UTC model.

faq.q: What makes New Jersey's rule against perpetuities unique?
faq.a: New Jersey has completely abolished the Rule Against Perpetuities for both real and personal property under N.J.S.A. 46:2F-9. The common law rule against perpetuities is not in force in New Jersey. This allows perpetual dynasty trusts of unlimited duration, making New Jersey a favorable jurisdiction for multi-generational wealth transfer planning without the time constraints found in states that retain the perpetuities rule.

faq.q: Does New Jersey impose an inheritance tax on trust distributions?
faq.a: Yes. New Jersey imposes an inheritance tax for certain beneficiary classes, specifically Class C and Class D beneficiaries. This is unique among states and affects trust distributions. The inheritance tax applies in addition to New Jersey's state income tax on trust income for resident trusts where at least one trustee is a New Jersey resident. Trust planners must account for these tax consequences when structuring New Jersey trusts.

faq.q: Can a New Jersey trust be modified or terminated under the UTC?
faq.a: Yes. The NJ UTC provides robust mechanisms for modification and termination of irrevocable trusts, including modification by consent of the settlor and qualified beneficiaries under N.J.S.A. 3B:31-27, modification due to unanticipated circumstances under 3B:31-28, and modification to achieve tax objectives. New Jersey also provides for virtual representation under 3B:31-15 et seq. and nonjudicial settlement agreements, though the state does not have a specific decanting statute.

blocks.common_mistakes: A common error is assuming that New Jersey's certification of trust follows the standard UTC model exactly. The NJ UTC does not require the trust's taxpayer identification number or the manner of taking title, only the name in which title may be taken. Another mistake is failing to include the statement that the trust has not been revoked, modified, or amended in any manner that would cause the representations to be incorrect. A certification signed by fewer than all currently acting trustees also fails the statute, which requires all persons identified as currently acting as trustee to sign. Under N.J.S.A. 3B:31-81, the certification must be signed by ALL persons identified as currently acting as trustee, not just any trustee.
blocks.state_notes: New Jersey adopted the Uniform Trust Code in 2015 (P.L. 2015, c. 276), effective January 1, 2016, codified in Title 3B of the New Jersey Revised Statutes. The NJ UTC closely follows the model UTC with state-specific modifications, particularly in fiduciary duties and beneficiary information rights. New Jersey's most notable trust law feature is the complete abolition of the Rule Against Perpetuities under N.J.S.A. 46:2F-9, allowing perpetual dynasty trusts. The state imposes an inheritance tax for certain beneficiary classes (Class C and D), which is unique among states. New Jersey also has a state income tax on trust income for resident trusts. The NJ UTC's requirement that ALL currently acting trustees sign the certification of trust is a notable departure from the model UTC. The state has a strong body of trust case law predating the UTC adoption and provides for virtual representation and nonjudicial settlement agreements.
